Russia would probably use the summit to nudge China and the US closer to Moscow’s positions on Ukraine , said Sun Yun, director of the China program at the Stimson Center. However, Trump has been warned by his advisers to steer clear of Ukraine as a topic of the discussions, said Danny Russel, a former senior state department official who served in Barack Obama’s administration and who is now a distinguished fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

Ukraine again came under attack from Russia on Saturday, after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy repeated his calls for allies to supply Kyiv quickly with missiles for the US-made Patriot system to defend Ukrainian cities . Zelenskyy on Friday had warned that the Ukrainian military was bracing for new ⁠strikes ​by Russian forces against important infrastructure. “We ⁠have intelligence at this time that Russia is preparing new strikes on energy, on ⁠bridges across the Dnipro, on civilian infrastructure,” Zelenskyy said ​in his nightly ‌video address. “The ‌air force and the armed forces of Ukraine ‌as a whole are preparing for defence. It will not be easy.”

Kyiv, along with other Ukrainian cities, has been subjected to near-constant attacks for several weeks. A missile attack by Russian forces ⁠early on Saturday damaged a residential ⁠building in the Ukrainian capital , according to Mayor ​Vitali ‌Klitschko. The city’s military administration, also writing on Telegram, said two people were injured and a building housing a kindergarten was ‌damaged. Officials continued to warn residents of the potential for more strikes hours ​after the attack.

President Zelenskyy says he wants specific guarantees from western allies on how postwar security support would function when the war with Russia finally ends . Zelenskyy’s comments in an interview aired late Thursday followed two days of discussions among allies in Brussels that focused on postwar security and reconstruction. They also came before planned three-way talks next week in Abu Dhabi between Ukraine, Russia and the United States, the first trilateral peace discussions since February. “What matters is that it’s clear on paper,” Zelenskyy said in an interview with Ukraine’s private 1+1 television broadcast late Thursday. “The question isn’t dozens of points, but simply an understanding of the outcome: If Russia starts [attacking] again, what will happen? Who will do what, with what means, and when?”

The Brussels meetings brought together officials from the US, UK, France, Germany and the European Union, along with representatives from the World Bank and the US investment group BlackRock , Ukrainian lead negotiator Rustem Umerov wrote in an online post. “We separately discussed the threats from Russia to Ukraine and all of Europe, as well as joint steps to counter them,” Umerov wrote.

stories.title: Ships loiter near subsea cables amid Iran's warnings to Trump
stories.summary: Iran threatened to attack subsea cables if US escalates military strikes again.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Iran threatened to attack subsea cables if US escalates military strikes again.

Several tanker ships linked to Iran have been loitering over subsea Internet cables in the Gulf of Oman near the Strait of Hormuz—a possible indication that the Iranian government is preparing to attack such undersea infrastructure in response to any renewed US and Israeli strikes.

The movements of three sanctioned tankers and an Iranian fishing boat have been tracked near major undersea cables by the maritime intelligence firm Windward in October, according to the Financial Times . Six active cables currently cross through the contested Strait of Hormuz, linking the Middle East to Europe, Africa and Asia, with two more cables having segments under construction in the region.

Four countries, including Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar, depend entirely upon such subsea telecommunications connections running through the Strait of Hormuz chokepoint to link with the outside world. But other countries also depend heavily on the region’s undersea cable network—one third of India’s westbound Internet traffic goes through the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz.

One cable under construction, the 2Africa cable , is owned by a tech consortium that includes the US company Meta. That was one of the major cable corridors visited by the drifting Iran-linked ships.

Windward used both ship-tracking data and satellite images to track the vessels as they slowed down and looped around near multiple cables, with some ships then “going dark” by switching off their automatic identification system (AIS) transponders that normally broadcast their location and other information.

Such movement and behavioral patterns suggest the Iran-linked ships may be “mapping the cable routes, or placing charges or mines on them while dark,” Windward told the Financial Times.

Windward highlighted the examples of two sanctioned tankers linked to Iran that spent days drifting “directly over regional cable corridors… both with no commercial reason to stop” in a blog post on October 26. Both ships carried no commercial cargo.

Threats of cable fees and attacks

Since the US and Israel first launched a major war with Iran in February 2026, Iran’s response beyond targeting US military bases, ships and aircraft has included attacking commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and hitting oil refineries and other energy infrastructure along with airports in various Gulf countries.

Iran has also made a point of threatening or attacking US Big Tech infrastructure in the Middle East, including launching multiple drone strikes on Amazon data centers . In May 2026, a spokesperson for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed Iran would “impose fees on Internet cables” belonging to US tech companies and other owners.

But more recently, multiple Iranian officials and commanders of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) have warned that they could directly attack the undersea cables running through the Strait of Hormuz. This came after President Donald Trump repeatedly threatened to renew major US military strikes on Iran and warned he could “annihilate” the country during a speech at the United Nations in New York on September 22.

“Seven major cables run through the Strait of Hormuz, supporting global Internet operations and commercial data transmission,” one IRGC spokesperson said on October 20. “We remind the enemy of this.”

The latest phase of the war has involved more limited US military strikes against Iranian targets, even as Trump has alternated between threats and touting the possibility of a diplomatic breakthrough. Meanwhile, Iran has increased drone strikes and other attacks on commercial ships to exert its own pressure on the United States, with October marking the highest number of ship attacks since the war began.

Much damage has already been done. The limited fleet of cable-laying ships used for installation and repair has not been able to venture safely into the region since the war began, which forced the Meta-backed 2Africa cable to pause its planned expansion . The war has also compelled US tech companies and Gulf countries to accelerate efforts to develop alternative cable routes bypassing the Strait of Hormuz.

The Middle East is not the only part of the world where threats to the Internet’s undersea backbone have intensified. Subsea infrastructure is increasingly at risk from sabotage and gray-zone warfare from the Baltic Sea to the Pacific Ocean.

In today’s newsletter: From the cost of living to the AI bubble and the fight against fascism, Weber answers Guardian readers’ questions on how to build a fairer economy and world

G ood morning. As stateside celebrations die down, the Democratic party will be forced to confront a (deceptively) simple question: now what? Their colossal midterm successes will curtail Trump’s power during his remaining time in office, but the battle to shape the Democratic platform heading into next year’s presidential primaries is only just getting started.

While rallying against Trump is one thing, sustaining support by making a tangible difference to the lives of voters struggling with the cost of living is another. It’s a challenge for progressive parties facing down the far right across the world.

For years, economist Isabella Weber has argued that progressive politicians can win back voters by focusing on a fundamental issue: make life’s necessities – housing, transport, food, water, energy, healthcare – affordable to all. It’s the basis of her new book, Anti-Fascist Economics , and her ideas have found a receptive audience in New York, where Zohran Mamdani, who has followed Weber’s work for years, has made affordability central to his agenda. Now, a raft of progressive candidates have won on similar platforms . Weber’s influence is also being felt in the UK, with Andy Burnham’s Labour conference speech echoing much of her messaging.

A few weeks ago, we asked you to send in questions for Weber. In today’s First Edition, she answers them. That’s after this morning’s headlines.

Five big stories

UK | Cocaine has overtaken heroin as the biggest cause of drug deaths in England and Wales, figures from the Office for National Statistics show.

France | Hundreds of thousands are expected to march in demonstrations across France as trade unions call for a nationwide strike expected to extend to hospital workers, air traffic control, the post office, teachers and rail staff.

Commonwealth summit | The UK has agreed to “structured dialogue” in the next year with Caribbean nations affected by the slave trade and its legacy, Commonwealth leaders have said.

US news | Pete Hegseth is increasingly looking like he may take the fall for Republicans’ midterm losses, despite Donald Trump’s vocal support for his defense secretary, even calling him a champion of war.

Ebola | A British healthcare worker with Ebola is being evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo to the UK for medical treatment, it has been confirmed.

Isabella Weber answers your questions

What are the most interesting or radical actions governments are taking to improve affordability in an increasingly volatile world? Jack in Ireland

IW: Mexico’s government has an agreement with grocery companies to fix the price of a basket of essential foods. President Claudia Sheinbaum is making clear that it is her responsibility to negotiate on behalf of ordinary people and make essentials affordable. This is the opposite of neoliberalism, which tells people that democracy is the greatest system, yet that elected officials can do little to meet their basic material needs. Mexico has also capped energy prices, guaranteed small-scale farmers minimum prices for staples to encourage domestic production, and built emergency buffer stocks.

Spain capped the price of gas for power generation, which effectively contained the 2022 energy shock, offered free commuter and regional rail passes while the crisis lasted, and established public scrutiny of corporate profits.

At the municipal level, Vienna stands out : around half of its residents live in municipal or subsidised housing. Istanbul has pioneered people’s canteens that offer nutritious meals at an affordable price point. And New York City has put affordability policies such as rent freezes, investment in housing stock and public supermarkets back on the international agenda.

﹡﹡﹡

How should these midterm results shape Democratic economic policies? Should they be cautious or bold? Jessica in Brighton, UK

The Democrats won votes on affordability , and now they must have the courage to deliver real change. A dignified life for all must be the north star and that requires a fundamental overhaul of the economic playbook. Last time the Democrats enjoyed an electoral wave was in 2008, and under Obama they then leaned into neoliberalism. Bidenomics got stuck in a halfway house.

This time, the economy needs to be rebuilt starting from the essentials – energy, food, housing, communication, transport, all forms of care – with investments that create meaningful and decent jobs. Short term measures such as price policies can buy time and build power to regain public control over the essentials on which our lives and industries depend. We must then change how we provide them so that provision is compatible with planetary boundaries while constraining corporate power.

﹡﹡﹡

Why do governments use interest rates to control inflation? It seems unfair and clumsy. Simon in Perth, Australia and James in Leeds, UK

We often say interest rate hikes cool down the labour market – it sounds nice, like a fresh breeze. But simply put, the goal of rate hikes is to curb inflation by increasing unemployment and weakening workers’ ability to demand high wages. Higher rates also raise the cost of investments, for example in renewable energy that would make our economies less vulnerable to future shocks, and they increase mortgage costs, deepening the housing affordability crisis. This causes considerable harm, potentially pushing people towards the far right.

That is why I argue for surgical, sectoral stabilisation policies for essentials that buy time for structural measures. Rate hikes remain the standard response, whatever the nature of inflation, because central banks are in charge of monetary stability and have only one instrument at their disposal. We need a new approach in which governments fight inflation too, and central banks take on new tasks such as monitoring profit margins and issuing early warnings about rising prices of essentials that can unleash inflation.

﹡﹡﹡

Why do economists accept 2 to 3% inflation as OK but not 0%? Wouldn’t consumers be better off if prices went down rather than up? Rich in Michigan, USA

The 2% target is an arbitrary rule of thumb for central banks, established relatively recently. But the idea that a little inflation supports steady growth is old. If purchasing power slowly declines, there is an incentive to invest or spend rather than hoard cash in your mattress. Moderate inflation also makes debt servicing easier, both for private borrowers and governments.

﹡﹡﹡

Why are we obsessed with economic ‘growth’? It seems to drive self-destructive behaviour. Richard in Hampshire, UK and Tim in Lewes, UK

This is a live debate, especially in the context of climate change. Capitalist economies are predicated on growth because capital always strives for greater profits, but growth does not automatically guarantee a dignified life. What I am arguing for is to replace this growth imperative with an affordability and full- employment imperative: essentials should be removed from profit fundamentalism and organised to ensure affordable provisioning for all, and the government should be responsible for guaranteeing decent and meaningful jobs.

﹡﹡﹡

I support a vigorous tax on wealth. Something like a 100% tax on all wealth over $1 b n. Do you agree? Bill in Virginia, USA

Roosevelt warned that “the liberty of a democracy is not safe if private power grows stronger than the democratic state itself: That, in its essence, is fascism-ownership of government by an individual, by a group, or by any other controlling private power.” This was a key lesson from the consolidation of the Nazis’ power. Taxing the ultra-rich to limit extreme wealth concentration is key to anti-fascist economics. A 100% tax on wealth over $1bn might, however, not be the best design. A progressive tax that limits wealth accumulation starting at somewhat lower levels would make it harder to amass a billion dollars to begin with.

﹡﹡﹡

What will happen if the AI bubble bursts? Fiona in Edinburgh, UK

The immediate impact would probably be a stock market crash and a financial crisis. But such a crisis would also present an opportunity to turn things around. Governments should not bail out the companies but socialise them and turn them into democratically controlled utilities.

AI has cannibalised humanity’s knowledge and automated it to make profits for a handful of companies that openly state their business could lead to human extinction; it should serve the common good instead. As it creeps into our work and we increasingly rely on it in our daily lives, we will have to take public control of AI while also creating space for knowledge creation and creativity that are not competing with AI services. Otherwise, exercising the mind will become a privilege of the wealthy few. Some questions have been condensed for clarity.

What else we’ve been reading

Having recently finished reading Yesteryear, I find myself perhaps more fascinated by trad wives than I’d like to be. Lucy Knight’s deep dive into the women leaving the movement, was excellent and eye opening. Poppy Noor, newsletters team

I love Coco Khan’s writing, so I made a beeline for her column on why celebrities wear tone-deaf Halloween costumes . In it, she unpicks “the strange, insulated life that comes with sustained wealth”, while being very funny and somehow, against all odds, hopeful?! Genius. Lucinda Everett, newsletters team

There are so many ways to put together a stunning portrait. I loved looking at this year’s gallery from the Winston Taylor Portrait Prize – call me basic, but my favourite is the six-year-old Elvis impersonator. Poppy

Our interview with Kathryn Hunter was heartbreaking and brave, done excellently by the warm and brilliant Paula Cocozza . Poppy

I am not one of those admirable souls who gets their Christmas shopping sorted with weeks to spare. But having realised there’s nothing in this gift guide that someone in my life wouldn’t love, I feel this could be the year I’m done and dusted by mid-November. Lucinda

Sport

Football | Liverpool surrendered their 100% Champions League record, losing 3-2 at Fenerbahce despite leading twice, while Arsenal held on to win 2-1 in Czechia.

Rugby union | The Six Nations and Sanzaar unions have agreed to sell all their media rights and commercial deals collectively for the first time in a new revenue-sharing model.

Golf | Rory McIlroy voiced his support on Wednesday for the DP World Tour chief executive’s claim that LIV Golf’s goal was to “destroy” the European golf circuit.

The front pages

“Trumped”, is the Guardian ’s front page headline today, while the FT goes with “Crushing midterm rebuke to Trump”, and the Times writes “Trump faces backlash as Democrats make history. The Telegraph writes “Vance turns on Trump”, similarly The i Paper has “Vance blames Trump’s war for crushing defeat”, and the Mail says “Maga turns on Trump”. The Mirror ’s headline is “Reborn in the U.S.A.”, and Metro writes “Lame Donald Duck”.

Elsewhere, the Express , on asylum seeker housing, has “You are not listening!” and the Sun leads on “Markle ‘filth stash No3’”.

The Latest

Democrats’ midterms triumph deals devastating blow to Trump’s Republicans

Democrats have won a historic sweep in the US midterm elections, winning back control of Congress in a major setback for Donald Trump. Senate seats went blue in traditional Republican strongholds like Texas, South Carolina and Kansas – which saw the first Democrat win since 1932. Voters have sent a strong message of discontent to the Trump administration over the economy, the cost of living and rising gas prices. Trump is now a lame duck president for the rest of his term as president. Lucy Hough speaks to Washington editor Ankita Rao.

Cartoon of the day | Martin Rowson

The Upside

A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

Phoebe Waller-Bridge, the creator of the hit show Fleabag, has bought and donated a London flat to Writers’ Block – a scheme tackling class barriers in theatre – so that early-career writers can live in the capital rent-free while they attend meetings, rehearsals, and other career opportunities.

Other high-profile creatives backing the scheme, which invites Londoners to offer spare rooms to writers at reduced rates, include Jack Thorne, who co-created Adolescence, and James Graham, who wrote the stage show Dear England.

“When I first made it to London, I slept on friends’ floors and worked in call centres … while I wrote,” says Graham. “Every spare room a scheme like this can give to writers starting out in London, not only helps them write but saves them from giving up completely.”

stories.title: Why smoky bacon crisps threaten to reignite rows over EU rules
stories.summary: A post-Brexit deal on food standards has raised questions over the future naming of the classic British snack.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 6 November 2026

The naming of smoky bacon-flavoured crisps has become the latest political headache to emerge from the government's bid for closer ties with the EU.

The government is negotiating a deal on food standards in a bid to cut costs for British companies trading with Europe.

Labour ministers have been keen to talk up the potential economic benefits of the agreement, which could be announced at a summit later this month.

But the deal's requirement for Britain to adopt EU food rules in a wide range of areas has threatened to reignite sovereignty debates from the Brexit era.

Labour ministers have been keen to sidestep talking about the impact of alignment in particular sectors, instead stressing the overall economic boost it expects the food deal to bring.

On Thursday, Environment Secretary Angela Eagle told a radio presenter he should "get a life" when he asked about the potential impact of the new rules on snacks, such as smoky bacon crisps.

But it highlights the political dangers for the government of realigning with regulations that British politicians have not been able to shape, with the Conservatives and Reform UK keen to pounce on cases showing Britain to be a "rule taker" from Brussels.

It is not the first regulatory skirmish over smoky bacon crisps - following previous headlines over how the well-loved British flavour could be affected by an EU decision in 2024 to phase out a number of artificial smoke flavourings.

Now, the flavour name itself has been called into question by a separate EU attempt to restrict how descriptions of meat are used to market food.

Under rules adopted this summer, the EU plans to restrict the use of 31 terms, including bacon, drumstick and steak, to products that contain meat, claiming consumers could be confused by plant-based alternatives using the same names.

The European snack industry is seeking clarity on how the rules, which will also cover terms such as pork, chicken and beef, would apply to meat-flavoured crisps, including those flavoured without the use of any meat extracts.

The UK government has said it expects the new regulations to be in scope of its proposed food standards deal.

This means they would also apply to companies marketing their products in Britain, which is among the biggest consumers of crisps in Europe, according to analysts Euromonitor. , external

Uncertainty over rules

It has raised the prospect that crisps with names such as smoky bacon and roast chicken could have to be relabelled to be sold in British shops, although much remains unclear about how the rules will apply in practice.

The new EU rules, which will not come into force until after August 2029, will allow the European Commission to create exemptions for meaty names with an established long-term use to describe other types of food product.

The Brussels-based body is yet to set out how it plans to use this power, or what it means for snacks.

A group of conservative German MEPs are also seeking a specific carve-out for meat names in snacks and sauces in separate legislation , external currently making its way through the European Parliament.

The Food and Drink Federation, which represents British crispmakers including Walkers and KP Snacks, has been supportive of the government's bid to reach a food deal due to its potential to reduce trade barriers with Europe.

But it has highlighted the new rules as an example of where it wants the government to work with industry to ensure UK interests are reflected in EU decision making.

"Meat protections are an example of a new EU rule that UK businesses will need to comply with, but which the UK was not involved in developing," added the body's chief scientific officer Kate Halliwell.

'Unintended consequences'

The Potato Processors' Association, which also represents a number of major snackmakers, said it was monitoring the situation closely and wanted to see clarification of how the rules could affect its members.

Vanessa Richardson, its deputy director general, said her association supported moves to reduce "unnecessary barriers" in the trade of food products.

But she added it was important that the government's deal is implemented in a way that "avoids unintended consequences for established product descriptions which consumers clearly understand as referring to a flavour".

The Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) says it stands ready to help British snack businesses prepare for the impact of the new EU rules.

It is not yet clear what a British version of the rules would look like, or whether they would need to apply from 2029 alongside the new European regulations.

In 2014 Burnham posted a supportive message on social media when Brand was facing media criticism about his housing arrangements

Published 6 November 2026

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said Russell Brand has rightly been held to account for his "horrific" crimes and sought to explain Labour's previous association with the comedian.

Some within the Labour Party attempted to court Brand's support more than a decade ago, before police began investigating him - and in 2014 Burnham posted a supportive message on social media when the comedian was facing media criticism about his housing arrangements.

Asked about the 2014 tweet on Friday, Burnham said: "It's not always the case that people know everything about people in public life."

Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault on Thursday.

In 2014, Brand was writing regular opinion pieces for newspapers and appearing on political discussion programmes, including the BBC's Question Time.

His anti-establishment and left-wing views had also gained him a following on social media.

The same year, Burnham, then the shadow health secretary, posted on Twitter in support of Brand following allegations about the comedian's housing arrangements.

It is not clear what Burnham had been referring to in his 2014 tweet, but the previous day, The Sun claimed Brand had paid rent at a property owned by a landlord in a tax haven, while at the same time campaigning against tax avoidance.

Brand threatened to sue the newspaper and said he would give the money to victims of the Hillsborough disaster, a group Burnham has long campaigned for.

At the time, Burnham said it was "depressing to see media mission to discredit someone who stops playing their game" and urged Brand to "keep going".

Asked about that social media post on Friday, Burnham told the BBC "all I can say is I had no idea of the full extent of what he was doing or what he went on to do".

The PM added: "His [Brand's] crimes are horrific, he's rightly been held to account, justice for the victims and that is the right course that's been taken here.

"It's not always the case that people know everything about people in public life, but what is important is that where there is wrongdoing it is exposed."

The prime minister added: "Credit to the victims, huge credit, the courage that it's taken, but also the journalists who've exposed this."

Ed Miliband, then the Labour leader, was interviewed by Brand in the run-up to the 2015 general election.

Brand, who had previously dismissed the idea of voting, backed Labour following the interview, saying Miliband had convinced him that "this bloke will listen to us".

Miliband, who is now foreign secretary, has previously said he regrets being interviewed by Brand .

On Friday, a spokesman for Miliband told the BBC: "These are horrific crimes that Russell Brand has been found guilty of and Ed's profound sympathy is with the victims.

"As he said in 2023, 'of course, knowing what I know now - and I was not aware of these allegations at the time about Russell Brand - I wouldn't have done that interview and I regret doing it'."

Brand was found not guilty of two other counts of rape, and one count of attempted indecent assault.

During a four-week trial, Brand faced allegations from six women spanning the decade between 1999 and 2009.

The 51-year-old was refused bail and will spend the weekend in custody before he is due to return to court on Monday for sentencing.

stories.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang summoned by Congress over Chinese espionage concerns
stories.summary: Lawmakers want answers about Jensen Huang’s ties to an alleged Chinese intelligence asset.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Lawmakers want answers about Jensen Huang’s ties to an alleged Chinese intelligence asset.

Top Republican lawmakers have asked Jensen Huang to appear before Congress to answer questions after it was reported that US intelligence officials believe Nvidia’s chief executive has been targeted by a Chinese spying operation.

The chairs of the House committees on China, foreign affairs, and intelligence wrote to Huang this week asking him to appear before a joint closed-door briefing for their committees on November 18.

“Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the People’s Republic of China’s access to sensitive US technology and information,” representatives John Moolenaar, Brian Mast, and Rick Crawford wrote.

“The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk,” the lawmakers added.

The New York Times last week wrote that US intelligence officials believed Huang had been the target of a Chinese spy operation. The concerns center on a Chinese woman named Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud company that has bought billions of dollars of Nvidia’s chips.

Nvidia has rejected the claims and on Thursday would not say if Huang would appear before Congress. “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job. Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the company said.

“Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information—not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets—and zero information relevant to national security,” it added.

The lawmakers said they wanted Huang to discuss the security protocols Nvidia had in place to protect against “foreign adversary espionage.” The company said its chief executive had an “outstanding security team” that travels with him.

The New York Times said Huang had not received a “defensive briefing,” which the intelligence community usually, but not always, provides potential espionage targets to warn them about the activity.

Nvidia said it was confident that the US government would have let the company know if it thought a person was a threat to US industry and that it often receives updates from Washington about people of concern.

The US has previously scrutinized Megaspeed, founded in 2023 as a spin-off from a Chinese gaming company, for potential chip smuggling, although no charges followed.

Nvidia launched its own unannounced on-site inspections at Megaspeed in Singapore when it became aware of the US concerns, but the internal probe found no evidence of its chips being diverted into China, said people familiar with the matter.

The company’s supply chain has come under increasing scrutiny as US export controls have prompted increased smuggling of its chips. Earlier this year Wally Liaw, a co-founder of Supermicro, one of Nvidia’s key supply chain partners, was arrested in the US and charged with smuggling Nvidia chips into China. He denies any wrongdoing and has pleaded not guilty.

stories.body:
Google is rightfully facing blowback for forcing K-12 schools to enable AI if they wanted to keep using Google search. The company quickly backtracked and decoupled and turned off the services by default, but made it clear search will continue to be just another AI chatbot. This mandate forces an ultimatum on educators: accept generative AI or de-google your school.

Students, teachers, and parents across the U.S. are now years into an argument about how schools should respond to the growth of AI-enabled tools. Google decided to skip this debate and take this choice from schools. In August it activated AI chatbot Gemini for 150 million K-12 students on Google Classroom, leaving educators scrambling to respond . A few months later, Google introduced a new way to turn it off — but now administrators would also be turning off Google search .

Google walked this back somewhat, clarifying that Gemini, Gemini notebook, and Search will have their own controls and will be off by default. But because of Google’s broader approach to force AI on all search users, this change is still an example of a tech monopolist pushing unwanted changes into the classroom.

Tying AI to Search

It’s no secret that the biggest companies in AI are operating at a huge loss , in the hope they can follow Uber’s enshittification playbook . Offer a cheap convenience at a major loss until old systems atrophy, then flip the script to reduce wages and raise consumer costs—whether that’s paying with cash or with data.

This puts Google in the odd position of an incumbent, with around 90% of search traffic . It needs to not only make good on its own AI investment, but protect its dominance from new AI tools. It’s not just enough to offer its own AI mode, it needs to turn search into AI mode, while engaging in clumsy self-preferencing that is eating its own ad revenue .

The problem with this approach is the public is split on AI, to put it mildly. Some users will welcome these changes, but the rest are stuck in an all-or-nothing bargain. Anyone concerned about the accuracy of AI overviews or their impact on click-through rates for online communities and small publishers can just deal with it . The bet is any inconvenience in switching to an alternative is enough to keep you trapped.

Google can and should offer a way to disable AI overviews. Smaller services like DuckDuckGo* and Brave search have simple and persisting AI settings which don’t require login. These services also don't mince words and make a distinction between generated AI summaries, suspected AI results, and the backend use of AI to curate links.

It’s not enough to point to opaque workarounds , either. Adding “-ai” to your Google search will usually remove AI Overview, but so will “-unicorn”. This trick isn’t meant to be an AI off-switch, it’s a quirk of how AI Overview was implemented and can change at any time. These tricks also don’t generalize well to settings for system administrators . Hacks might work for now, but everyone—including administrators—deserve clear set-and-forget controls for the tools they rely on.

Pushing AI on Schools

De-googling your life isn’t easy, and for schools it can be even more difficult. For decades Google has gone after schools to foster life-long Google users—resulting in many institutions being deeply entrenched in its ecosystem despite data privacy concerns . That’s because schools face major switching costs when moving to a competitor. It takes more than flipping a setting—it means a lengthy contract process, staff retraining, and a cumbersome migration of past work.

The difficulty of switching makes granular controls even more essential, particularly for a hot-button issue like generative AI. Few parents would send their kids to AI-driven schools , but they may want their kids to learn tools like search as they exist outside of the classroom. However, many parents and teachers concerned with AI disrupting learning are pushing major school districts to implement temporary AI moratoriums for young students. These pauses are meant to make sure any introduction of AI fits the needs of students and is done in a way that actually makes sure educators are prepared.

But in either camp, this is a choice that must be made by schools, not Google. Teachers know more about what their students need than a trillion-dollar tech company, and this expertise should be respected in their own classrooms.

Google’s self-preferencing and desperate attempt to eventually recoup on an AI money pit must be tempered with more fine-tune controls over generative AI. It’s in Google’s own interest to stop abusing its dominance to piss off users, advertisers, and school communities. It’s also Google’s responsibility as an adjudicated monopolist.

stories.body:
My friend was due to be released next January. Under draconian security laws, his sentence has been extended by 10 years

T wo years ago, I wrote in this newspaper about the lengthy imprisonment of my friend Joshua Wong, who I spent years campaigning alongside for the advancement of Hong Kong’s democracy. He was given an unjust sentence meant to keep him behind bars until January 2027. He was supposed to be released in a few months, when I hoped he would finally be able to reunite with his friends and family and embark on a new chapter.

But this hope was misplaced. The end of the tunnel isn’t next year; it’s late 2036. By then, he will be 40. On Thursday, Joshua was sentenced to another 10 years under Hong Kong’s national security law for colluding with foreign forces. He is the only political prisoner who’s been convicted twice under the national security law. The judge described Joshua and me as “two ringleaders or masterminds” urging foreign powers to impose sanctions and other hostile actions against the Chinese and Hong Kong governments. The judgment cited previous international advocacy work, media interviews, social media posts and the political activities of Demosistō, the youth-led democratic party we founded.

Much of the cited evidence predates the implementation of the national security law, even though the court insisted it was not being applied retrospectively. Before 2020, meeting with foreign parliamentarians, engaging with and speaking to international institutions, and advocating for measures against human rights abuses were ordinary campaign strategies. These were peaceful means through which we tried to hold those in power accountable. The campaigns raised the profile of Hong Kong’s protests and garnered substantial support; they were so effective that Beijing had to impose the national security law to curb them and impose extensive legal punishments.

There is a stark lack of evidence about Joshua’s actions. Prosecutors said that he conspired with campaigners including myself to ask foreign bodies to impose sanctions on China – relying on his sharing of Facebook posts written by me. But these posts did not directly call for sanctions – they made other appeals, including for digital forensic companies to terminate their cooperation with the Hong Kong police. There’s no evidence that Wong himself advocated for imposing any form of sanctions, or that he had any direct link to advocacy work outside Hong Kong. The court also accepted that no organisation or funding supported his activities after the law came into force.

Still, as flimsy as the evidence is, it’s enough to secure him a decade in jail. The crux of the trial is not legal; it’s political. It is clear that Beijing exercises sweeping control over Hong Kong’s legal and political systems. This can be seen in the tightening of the electoral system by introducing an Iranian-style vetting mechanism , in the jailing of peaceful political dissidents and the emphasis placed on the necessity of “patriots ruling Hong Kong” .

When Chinese leaders categorise Jimmy Lai, Benny Tai and Joshua Wong as the “masterminds” behind the 2019 pro-democracy protests, the legal system must deliver sentences that reflect the trio’s “importance” . That’s why Lai and Tai have been sentenced to 20 years and 10 years respectively, and rank among the most persecuted pro-democracy figures in the region. There are now close to 2,000 political prisoners in Hong Kong.

It’s devastating that Joshua has been behind bars for such a large portion of his adult life. I couldn’t even imagine skipping 16 years before I reached my 40s – during which time many people meet their partner, get married, raise a family and settle into a career. Joshua has been deprived of living fully because of his advocacy for important democratic values. The sentence signals to the world that China is determined to quash any hopes for freedom and democracy on its soil.

As geopolitical competition intensifies and populism rises, human rights are increasingly treated as an inconvenience to diplomatic and economic interests. Governments speak of stability and pragmatic engagement, while political prisoners slowly disappear from international public attention. The Chinese regime has little reason to change its approach if the repression of Hong Kong carries no meaningful consequences, either to trade or its global standing.

Given that Hong Kong was a British colony until as recently as 1997, the UK, in particular, should not regard the territory as merely another foreign policy issue. The Sino-British joint declaration was intended to safeguard the city’s rights and freedoms. The British government should therefore make the release of Joshua, Jimmy Lai and other political prisoners a priority when dealing with Beijing, rather than responding to each new sentence with another ineffective statement of concern.

For months, I had imagined the day Joshua would finally be free. Now that hope has been pushed away for another decade. We must not forget him, and must take urgent action to demand his immediate release.

stories.title: Presenting 'Desire Lines: Encoding Queer Digital Futures'
stories.summary: What does the digital future look like? Who gets to imagine it, shape it, and make it real? Building a freer, more inclusive digital age requires not only challenging systems of surveillance and control, but also making space for creativity, community, and radical imagination. That's why earlier this year with the queer arts collective , we put out a call for submissions inviting people to explore the intersections of technology, identity, and digital liberation—whether that involved pointing the lens towards an underrepresented issue in digital justice efforts; sharing personal accounts of joy, pleasure, or sorrow under surveillance; or painting wide imaginations for our communities using technology for good instead of carcerality and doom. And we’re excited to share that the project is now live! Desire Lines: Encoding Queer Digital Futures explores a digital world that dreams wilder and exists louder. Seven artists share their visions of digital liberation, spanning from early internet-coded yearning to escapist steamy chat rooms and seed-laced battle suits for revolution. These essays and stories remind us that digital rights aren't just about the existence of technology and its deployment as existing in a vacuum, but instead about how tech tools are a way for people to express themselves freely, find communities, explore identities, and build spaces to exist and seek joy without fear. Too often, conversations about technology focus on innovation, efficiency, and the next big thing while overlooking the people and communities most affected by the systems being built. This project was an effort to break containment and make space for something different: a chance to imagine digital futures rooted in queer creativity, resistance, and possibility. Together with the queer arts collective, we were excited to launch the magazine and celebrate the artists and ideas that brought it to life through our session at Mozilla Festival last week, ‘ Privacy x Queer Desire ,’ where we started out by co-curating a community privacy plan grounded in digital fairness before launching the magazine. Base rate increases from 3.75% and Bank governor signals another rise in near future to combat rising inflation

Analysis: Interest rate rise in midst of cost of living crisis will leave many incredulous

The Bank of England has raised interest rates for the first time in three years and warned of another increase to combat inflationary pressure unleashed by the Iran war.

Eight members of the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) voted for the rise, which takes the base rate from 3.75% to 4%. The ninth member, Catherine Mann, preferred a more dramatic half-point increase.

The Middle East conflict has pushed oil prices persistently above $100 a barrel in recent months, as hopes have evaporated of a deal that could reopen the strait of Hormuz .

As a result, the Bank now expects UK inflation to rise to 4.9% in the middle of next year – up from 3.2% in its last economic forecast in July. Inflation hit 3.5% in September , as measured on the consumer prices index.

The decision, which will hit mortgage borrowers, comes a week after John Healey used his first budget to promise “breathing space” for hard-pressed consumers. Echoing the Office for Budget Responsibility’s gloomy forecasts for living standards , the MPC expects real post-tax income to fall this year and next.

The Bank’s governor, Andrew Bailey , raised the prospect of another rate rise in the near future – with a resolution to the Iran conflict the key factor that will influence the decision.

“Without news which softens the risks to inflationary pressures, I can see the argument for a further increase in rates and thereafter taking a more conditional approach,” he said, according to the MPC minutes.

However, he played down the likelihood of a prolonged series of increases, as markets have been predicting. “Today’s increase shouldn’t be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence in hikes. But unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, neither does it seem likely to be the last increase,” he said.

The Bank’s next interest rate decision will be announced on 17 December, and some analysts suggested the MPC could press ahead with a pre-Christmas hike.

Andrew Goodwin, the chief economist at consultancy Oxford Economics , said: “The degree of inflationary pressure already in the system means another hike in December or February is likely.”

Explaining its decision to raise borrowing costs, the MPC highlighted the pass-through from elevated oil prices to business and consumer costs across the economy. It expects the Ofgem energy cap to rise from the equivalent of £1,723 a year for an average household in Great Britain to £2,150 in January and to increase again in April. Food price inflation could hit 4.75% by mid-2027, it warned.

Businesses have so far reported in the Bank’s surveys that they have been able to absorb soaring oil and gas prices – by hedging their energy costs, for example – but the MPC believes they will soon have to start passing them on to consumers in higher prices.

It is also concerned about workers seeking to offset the impact of the higher cost of living by asking for bumper pay rises.

after newsletter promotion

Oil prices have fallen sharply, to below $100 a barrel, after the Democrats’ victories in the US Congress, which some investors have interpreted as potentially constraining Donald Trump’s capacity to prolong the conflict in Iran. Trump’s vice-president, JD Vance, has blamed the war, and its impact on inflation, for the rout at the polls.

Speaking at the Bank’s press conference, Bailey welcomed the sharp fall in energy prices in the last 48 hours but said it would need to be sustained to change his view about the need for future rate rises. “This is positive news, but there is already a significant amount of inflationary pressure in the pipeline,” he said, adding: “What is the best thing that can happen? It is to resolve the conflict in the Middle East.”

While the decision to increase rates was supported by all MPC members, the minutes of the meeting reveal stark divisions over how much further they may need to go to bring inflation under control. The dovish Alan Taylor suggested this should be a “risk-management ‘one-for-now’ insurance hike”, while Mann argued that an immediate half-point rise was necessary to restore the Bank’s inflation-fighting credibility.

Healey’s budget included measures aimed at cushioning the impact of higher energy prices – including extending the fuel duty freeze and the VAT cut on electricity bills. The MPC said the package would shave a quarter percentage point off inflation in mid-2027.

Responding to the interest rate increase, Healey said: “The Iran conflict is reaching deep into the pockets of families and businesses here at home.

“In my budget I acted to give some breathing space to families and businesses. Twenty million households will get a £100 energy payment, I extended the tax cut on electricity bills and froze fuel duty. I also set out the course ahead to get costs down for good.”

But the shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, called the rate rise “another headwind for hardworking families to deal with”.

stories.body:
Polling done for the Guardian shows plummeting support from a former key constituency of Donald Trump’s base

Q&A: Ask your questions about Democrats’ win in the midterms

Polling conducted by the Harris Poll for the Guardian before the election shows just how angry voters were and points to one key reason Republicans lost so badly: plummeting support from rural voters, once a key constituency of Donald Trump’s base.

Over the summer, 95% of Americans indicated they believed there was an affordability crisis , particularly because of steep gas and grocery prices. By October, 61% of voters believed the country was experiencing a recession, even though technically it wasn’t.

It’s hard to ignore the impact inflation has had on this election. Key voters had expressed for months deep discontent with what had become the status quo. Loggers in Maine said that tariffs against Canada were hurting their already-battered industry. Drivers in Texas facing three-hour commutes to work were spending $400 a month on gas. Farmers across the midwest said diesel prices were exacerbating a growing season beleaguered by drought.

Recent data showed the flip wasn’t just seen among Democrats and independents, who have held pessimistic views on the economy since Trump returned to office, but among some Republicans, too.

In February, right before the war in Iran began, 49% of Republicans said the economy was getting better. By October, that number would drop to just 28%.

The pain seemed especially acute for rural voters, long considered a core base for Trump.

The president had gained many of his supporters by angling himself as a successful businessman who would be an outsider in Washington. But soaring gas and diesel prices have been a major pain point in parts of the country where driving long distances is an everyday part of life.

Rural voters were much more likely to say that gas prices were hurting their finances and that they were in economic “survival mode”, or that one surprise bill could sink them, compared with their urban and suburban counterparts. They were also slightly more likely to say that Republicans had a bigger problem with corruption, or elected officials using their position for personal financial gain, than Democrats.

In the month before the midterms, the number of rural Americans who said the economy was getting worse climbed 17% since Trump took office, compared with a 5% increase for those in the suburbs and a 3% jump among urban voters.

Yet on the eve of the midterm elections, Trump was trying to speak a different reality into existence, one where gas prices were going down, wages were rising and the US’s trade with other countries had never been stronger.

“I’ve traveled all across the country, spoken at all of these rallies I’ve done over the last two and a half weeks, and America is ready to go. They’re ready to vote,” Trump said in front of the Lincoln Memorial’s Reflecting Pool on Monday. “I hope they’re ready to do the right thing.”

But the reality that Americans have been facing is vastly different, and Americans responded accordingly. Republicans in key races from Maine to Texas lost their toss-up races on Tuesday, and Democrats will have control of Congress for the next two years.

Democrats have promised they will be busy trying to address the issues that were at the forefront of the election: the Trump administration’s brutal immigration crackdown, corruption in the White House, rising healthcare costs and the economy, specifically higher prices.

Republicans are just starting to take stock of the role prices had on the election outcome. JD Vance on Wednesday said the loss was the “cost to pay” for the Iran war. “Any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there,” Vance said.

As much as the midterms were a “blue-nami” for Democrats, pre-midterm polls showed voters were still unsure about the party’s ability to deal with affordability. When asked which party had the solution to the affordability crisis a month before the election, 34% said that neither party had a solution. Democrats (27%) slightly edged out Republicans (24%), but many voters seemed unsure whether any party could deal with these pocketbook issues.

Similar polling conducted before the 2024 presidential election showed that key independent voters were feeling just as pessimistic about the economy. Inflation had reached a generational high in 2022, and many Americans felt that Biden and Democrats weren’t doing enough.

Price increases under Trump, particularly after the Iran war, have only gotten worse. But many voters are dealing with years of economic burnout and will expect results in the coming years.

US tech stocks open higher after Thursday's rout

Ding ding goes the Wall Street opening bell, and trading is underway after the US stock market’s most bruising day in 19 months yesterday.

And it’s a mixed picture!

Tech stocks are rising, lifting the Nasdaq up by 1.2% in early trading. AI-linked stocks such as AMD (+8.1%), SanDisk (+8.3%) and Nvidia (+6.5%) are among the top risers.

But the much-storied Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA) is moving the other way, down 1% at the open. It’s being dragged down by old-economy stocks such as Nike (-3.5%), Walmart (-3.2%) and McDonalds (-3.1%).

Reminder: Yesterday the Nasdaq index slumped by 5.5%, while the DJIA dropped by 3.44%. So this is only a small recovery for the Nasdaq , and further pain for the Dow .

Nasdaq posts fourth weekly fall in a row

And finally…. the Nasdaq’s mini-recovery from its post-midterms plunge is complete.

The main US tech index has closed for the night up 1.09%, with a gain of 264 points to end at 24,579 points.

But the broader picture is that the Nasdaq Composite has now fallen for four weeks running, as some of the air has come out of the AI bubble…

We’ll find out on Monday whether the recovery continues, or the sell-off resumes…. Goodnight. GW

Tech stocks still higher in afternoon trading

A late update: With two hours to go before Wall Street closes, the tech rebound continues.

The Nasdaq Composite index, which sank into ‘correction territory’ yesterday, is up 1.3% now.

Aerospace manufacturer and launch service provider Rocket Lab are the top riser, up 12.5%, followed by Airbnb (+11.7%), AppLovin (+10%), Advanced Micro Devices (+9.3%) and Intel (+8.9%).

But…. Fawad Razaqzada, market analyst at Stonex Trading and FOREX.com, says AI concerns linger, explaining:

double quotation mark Technology stocks staged a sharp recovery on Friday after yesterday’s brutal sell-off wiped trillions of dollars off global equity valuations. All major AI-related stocks – Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom and Core Weave – bounced back. But whether recovery holds is another matter. After Thursday’s brutal sell-off wiped trillions of dollars off global equity valuations. Today’s bounce has carried the Nasdaq 100 straight back into former support, and the worries behind the rout, from AI regulation to the sheer scale of tech spending, have not gone away. With the index still carving out lower highs and lower lows, we maintain a cautious Nasdaq 100 forecast, and the near-term risk remains tilted to the downside.

Here’s a late take on this week’s sell-off, from Lee Robinson, CIO of Altana Downside Protector Fund and founder of Altana Wealth:

double quotation mark “This sell off has been a long-time coming, and it is not just caused by the midterms or an unwinding of positions in the tech giants. What we are seeing today is the result of stretched valuations and last month’s re-pricing in credit markets, specifically the rising Credit Default Swaps of the Magnificent Seven and CoreWeave. Credit is the engine of capital markets which equities will always eventually follow. We launched the Altana Downside Protector to trade a major downturn that we could see playing out over the next 18 months. The key questions now are who gets hurt by this selloff and what happens next. We see a lot of risk being held by life insurers who are some of the largest owners of AI-linked private credit funds and could be facing a series of de-ratings across their balance sheets.”

[Credit default swaps are an insurance contract that pays out if a company defaults on its debt, as covered in The Big Short ].

Closing post

With European stock markets closed after a nervy day, and Wall Street calmer than yesterday, it’s time to wrap up…

European stock markets fell sharply today as a rout in US tech stocks spread across the Atlantic, after the Democrats’ midterms victory sparked fears of a slowdown in the AI industry.

A sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday was followed by sharp falls in Asian stocks markets overnight. The investor sentiment then reached London, where the market was, at one stage, poised for its worst day since March.

The FTSE 100 index, which tracks blue-chip shares listed in London, was down as much as 254 points, or 2.35%, at 10,528 points during a wave of selling in morning trading. But by the close of the day it had recovered to a 1% fall, helped by a bounce in US stocks when Wall Street reopened.

Across Europe, there were similar losses: Germany’s Dax index has fallen by 2%, France’s Cac 40 has lost 0.8%, and Spain’s Ibex ended the day down 0.6%. Italy’s FTSE Mib fell 0.9%.

In Asia-Pacific markets, Japan’s Nikkei 225 index sunk 6% and South Korea’s Kospi index tumbled more than 6.5%.

“It’s actually a bit of a disaster,” said Christopher Forbes, the head of Asia and Middle East at CMC Markets.

double quotation mark “[Clients] were long index, long stocks, and they all got carried out. All night, all day – we had client margin calls, client complaints … because it’s a very emotional thing, right? People are wedded to their positions and views on a stock or outcome, and you’re telling them: ‘Look, you’ve just lost money.’”

Over in New York right now, the Nasdaq is up 1.5% (having fallen by 5.5% yesterday), and the S&P 500 is up 0.7%.

double quotation mark “Trading interest in overseas AI and technology companies has been growing all week. Bank’s decision goes contrary to analysis from Office for Budget Responsibility that predicts lower inflation and little impetus for wage growth

Bank of England raises interest rates to 4%

Business live – latest updates

An interest rate rise by the Bank of England to 4% is a big call when households are suffering from a second cost of living crisis in four years.

Many people will be incredulous when they hear of the decision to increase the cost of borrowing by 0.25 percentage points, looking around their neighbourhood for signs of a booming economy.

The official figures show the economy has proved resilient in response to the jump in oil and gas prices after the outbreak of war in Iran, but UK high streets are struggling and the underlying drivers of inflation are absent.

Most households are spending to stand still, whether it is on food, energy, holidays or leisure pursuits. Businesses are in much the same position. Like households, they have absorbed significant tax rises.

What the Bank’s policymakers believe is that despite all this, the energy price shock, being larger than first estimated, will surge through all parts of the economy, forcing up prices, encouraging a wave of wage demands that will, in turn, give inflation a second burst of life next year and the following year.

This analysis stands in contrast to the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), which acts as the Treasury’s independent forecaster. The OBR was clear in evidence to parliament on Wednesday that there was little impetus for strong wages growth.

The OBR said that, rather than economic growth next year of 1.6% and a rise in inflation to 4.9%, as the Bank expects, it believes the economy will expand by just 1% in 2027 and that the consumer prices index (CPI) will peak at just 3.75%. Inflation hit 3.5% in September, official figures showed .

The OBR’s chief economist, David Miles, said one of the main reasons for this assessment was the state of UK businesses, which he judged to be quite weak.

He said they had absorbed a large slice of the rise in energy and fuel costs, and their profit margins had plummeted on average as a result. Where once margins averaged 13% to 14%, the latest figures show they have fallen to 10% to 11%.

He said there would be little appetite to pay high wage settlements and the imperative would be to rebuild margins.

The wider economic situation is also very different from the previous crisis in 2022, when the country was coming out of the pandemic and dealing with the onset of the Ukraine war.

Back then, households were awash with lockdown savings that they wanted to spend, and firms were struggling to hire enough staff, leading to intense competition for workers and a spike in wages.

Today, savings are low and households bear the scars of four years of high inflation.

What sectors of the economy are making hay in 2026? Retailers and hospitality businesses are suffering, transport companies are battered by high costs and the charity sector is facing widespread financial difficulties. Vacancies are low, suggesting that firms have no need to employ more people.

Businesses in better-performing sectors such as banking and oil and gas also show little appetite for big wage increases. Banks are using artificial intelligence to shed staff .

The deputy director of the British Chambers of Commerce, David Bharier, said he was dismayed by the decision.

“So far, there is little sign of the wage-price spiral the Bank is looking to guard against. Unemployment is higher than in 2022, the labour market is looser and our research shows AI adoption accelerating rapidly – with some of the deepest users more likely to expect headcount reductions,” he said.

“After a budget which gave businesses little incentive to invest, and with borrowing costs already high, it is economic growth that will pay the premium.”

The Bank’s own survey of businesses and a separate report from its regional agents indicate “that wage and price expectations have moved little since September”.

It means Threadneedle Street policymakers judge that responses to their own business review will prove inaccurate and wages will jump.

The Bank judged that households’ and firms’ “attentiveness” to rising inflation was high and “there was a risk wage settlements would be higher than businesses expect”.

When the government says it is constrained by the bond markets from spending more to help consumers, there is a scenario looming in which ministers and the central bank, to meet their individual mandates, effectively crush the prospects for economic growth.

John Healey will say, as he did at the dispatch box last week, that he needs to restrict borrowing and adhere to his fiscal rules. Meanwhile, the bank will be busy making sure it cracks down on inflationary pressures it believes are on the way, even if policymakers cannot see them quite yet.

stories.body:
The latest UN climate summit, Cop31, will get underway in Antalya, Turkey, on November 9. One of its key objectives is to boost electrification across the global economy – replacing petrol and diesel vehicles, gas boilers and some industrial processes that burn fossil fuels with electric alternatives.

The summit’s host, Turkey, has set a target of 35% of energy demand being met by electricity by 2035, up from around 20% today. Announcing the “35-by-35” pledge, Cop31 president Murat Kurum described it as “one of the defining features” of Turkey’s presidency, highlighting the risks of continued dependence on imported fossil fuels .

Without doubt, electrification is essential to curtailing greenhouse gas emissions, and is already gathering pace. The International Energy Agency (IEA) has declared we are living in the “age of electricity” , and if stated policy pledges hold, global electrification rates will hit 31% by 2050. The Cop31’s focus on electrification hopes to build upon and accelerate this existing trend.

But electrification alone won’t deliver a clean energy transition. Two major challenges remain: the continued expansion of fossil fuel production, and growing geopolitical competition over clean technologies where the latter is increasingly shaping governments’ climate and energy policies, as they struggle to compete with dominant “electrostates” such as China.

Silence on supply

The Australian climate minister and Cop31’s president of negotiations has described electrification and fossil fuel reduction as “different sides of the same coin” . But they are not interchangeable. Electrification can reduce some demand for fossil fuels, but it won’t stop governments approving new projects and expanding supply.

By 2030, governments are planning to produce more than double the amount of fossil fuels than would be consistent with limiting warning to 1.5°C. More concerning is that this assessment was made before the conflict and disruption in the Middle East, which has caused the US, Brazil, Guyana, Argentina, Canada and other fossil fuel producers to increase output in the name of energy security. The UK, meanwhile, has approved the Jackdaw gasfield in a purported bid to protect jobs and keep homes warm.

The 35-by-35 target is also silent on where that additional electricity will come from. After all, a country could in theory increase its rate of electrification by burning more fossil fuels (imagine a country where every car was electric, but all that electricity came from coal).

A genuine energy transition

What’s needed is the two-pronged approach of electrifying economies while simultaneously phasing out fossil fuels and reducing their supply. This will ensure capital is reallocated to renewable energy for electrification. Governments can do this nationally or through international initiatives such as the Beyond Oil and Gas Alliance , the Clean Energy Transition Partnership and the Cop-adjacent conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels .

Skirting the fossil fuel issue is nothing new at these summits. It took 26 years for a formal resolution or agreement to explicitly name fossil fuels, in Glasgow in 2021 . And even then it only passed with calls to “phasedown” unabated coal power and phase-out “inefficient” fossil fuel subsidies.

At Cop31, fossil fuels are entirely absent from the formal agenda . Brazil has published an extensive voluntary “roadmap” to guide governments’ phase-out efforts, but this sits outside the formal negotiations and lacks timelines .

This begs the question: is a focus on electrification a way to avoid the perennially thorny issue of fossil fuels?

Just electrify everything

Even growing demand for electricity does not guarantee a clean energy transition. The data centre boom in the US and beyond, for instance, is driving the use of gas and coal to generate electricity. The International Gas Union, a lobby group for natural gas producers, is explicitly positioning gas as a way to meet growing demand from data centres and AI.

Increasing electrification looks relatively straightforward: just encourage more renewable energy production and electric vehicles . Yet, for most of the world, this would mean overcoming security and trade tensions with China, whose dominance in clean technologies, manufacturing and rare earth processing makes it a lynchpin electrostate in a world hoping to electrify everything.

China’s dominance is near total. For the component materials of solar panels, in 2024 China controlled 93% of global polysilicon processing, 97% of wafer manufacturing – making the thin slices of silicon that form the basis of solar panels – 92% of solar cell manufacturing and 86% of solar module production. It also produced more than 80% of electric vehicle batteries in 2025. According to the IEA, China is dominant across 19 of 20 energy-related strategic minerals, averaging over 70% of processing control. Achieving global electrification targets will therefore require continued access to Chinese technologies, products and raw materials.

This runs counter to almost two decades of western policy aimed at protecting domestic industries from Chinese competition and restricting China’s technological development, most notably with semi-conductors . While these efforts have largely failed to contain Chinese innovation, an overreliance on Chinese clean technologies is increasingly seen as a “serious risk” to Europe’s economic and national security. European governments have responded with tariffs and restrictions on Chinese imports and investments, while seeking to build up their own manufacturing capacity.

Governments face a difficult dilemma. Opening their economies further to Chinese technologies could mean unpicking trade protections developed over years and create new dependencies, while refusing to cooperate with China risks slowing electrification and may even drive some governments to abandon climate and energy policies altogether because they cannot compete.

While the drive towards electrification at Cop31 is to be welcomed, it cannot be a substitute for the harder political task of securing binding commitments to phase out fossil fuels, fast and fairly.

stories.body:
For decades, competing global development models have shaped sub-Saharan Africa’s agricultural landscape. Traditional western donors, such as the Norwegian Agency for Development Cooperation ( Norad ), have promoted climate-smart agricultural systems such as conservation agriculture , working through non-governmental organisations . Emerging donors, such as China, champion commercial, market-driven models through private-sector contract farming. They tend to focus on high-yielding export cash crops such as cotton.

Zambia is a good place for studying these dynamics. Donor aid remains critical. The country’s agricultural investment needs exceed the financial resources available from government budgets, domestic financial institutions and private investors. In 2024, the government budget allocation to agriculture, fisheries and livestock was ZMW 13.83 billion (US$528 million), which was 7.8% of the national budget. In the same year, the country received US$108 million in international development financing for its agricultural sector.

As food systems and development researchers at the University of Zambia, we set out to examine whether the origin of aid matters to the outcome. Does it influence whether a rural family has enough food to eat, or do local socio-ecological realities and farming practices matter more?

The role of agriculture is hugely important in Zambia. The agricultural sector accounts for 60% of total national employment. About 70% of the population relies on agriculture for its livelihoods, income and household food security.

Our study examined how top-down foreign aid approaches interact with agrarian realities in eastern Zambia. We aimed to disentangle the relative impacts of donor affiliation (Norwegian versus Chinese aid) and farming systems (conservation agriculture versus conventional farming) on household food security. Conservation agriculture is characterised by minimal soil disturbance, permanent soil cover, and crop rotations that include legumes. Conventional agriculture involves ploughing or ridging and may focus on growing a single crop in the same field for a long time.

Our research produced four main findings:

localised farming practices drive household food security and resilience, far outweighing donor identity

conservation agriculture achieves better food security outcomes than conventional agriculture

low crop diversity makes farmers vulnerable

food insecurity remained deeply structural, affecting women-headed households most.

We concluded from our findings that sustainable agrarian transitions require interventions that address systemic inequalities, particularly in relation to women, and empower locally adapted, ecologically diverse farming systems such as mixed farming systems.

Local farming practices outweigh donor identity

For our study we surveyed over 545 smallholder households in Chipata and Mambwe districts. Eastern Zambia has a variety of climate regions, and both models – the Norwegian-backed conservation projects and Chinese-backed contract farming – operate there.

Read more: Are Chinese investors grabbing Zambian land? Study finds that’s a myth

We started studying the projects in 2014, as part of a project examining donor aid effectiveness in Zambia and Malawi, and continued engaging with the question over the years. We asked farmers about their farming practices, their households, and their food security. In these communities, men are seen as the primary landowners and household heads. About half the households reported that they had not had enough food in the past 12 months.

We report four key findings.

Local farming systems override donor identity

After controlling for farming practices and geographic context, we found that donor affiliation made little difference to food security outcomes. Smallholder conservation agriculture improved food security outcomes by minimising climate risk and increasing crop yields. In contrast, donor aid projects tend to focus on predefined goals that rarely account for local environmental and socio-cultural conditions.

Conservation agriculture drives resilience

Farmers who adopted conservation agriculture achieved better food security outcomes than those using conventional agriculture. Conservation agriculture households consumed a broader range of foods from different food groups, such as carbohydrates, animal proteins, plant proteins, dairy, vegetables and fruits.

Conservation agriculture also proved vital for bridging the lean season . This is the period before harvest, between December and March, when farming households run out of grains from the previous harvest. Where farmers got help to prepare land earlier, they also harvested earlier (nine days before conventional farmers).

Export monocultures are risky

Donors that wanted commercial outcomes created new vulnerabilities. Chinese-backed initiatives, focused primarily on cotton contract farming, provided input loans in exchange for exclusive crop sales. While this model created market opportunities, it also reduced crop diversity. Households under Chinese-backed projects cultivated an average of 2.98 crops, compared with 3.63 under Norwegian-backed programmes that emphasised crop diversification. In drought-prone areas, tying farmers to a single export crop without supporting food crops or agroforestry stripped households of their traditional ecological safety nets.

Structural inequities and blind spots remain

Across all sample groups, female-headed households recorded lower dietary diversity and held fewer assets such as fruit trees and livestock. Cultural norms and patriarchal land tenure systems restrict women’s access to fertile land, extension services and agricultural labour.

When female farmers adopted conservation agriculture despite these barriers, their self-reported food security improved.

Neither Norwegian nor Chinese projects made livestock husbandry part of their interventions. Their models ignored a vital part of local mixed-farming systems that provides animal protein, organic manure, draught power and alternative income during crop failures. Mixed farming systems are more resilient in this region, where dependence on rain-fed agriculture is the norm.

Rethinking aid

Our study identified three strategies that could improve the effectiveness of donor aid in building rural resilience. Development partners and policymakers can:

support crop diversification, soil conservation and agroforestry rather than single export cash crops

explicitly address women’s access to secure land tenure, extension services and labour-saving tools

integrate livestock husbandry into aid portfolios alongside crop production.

Read more: Direct support to small scale farmers reduces poverty – what Zambia is doing right

Overall, international development agencies must move away from rigid, top-down blueprints. Simply changing a donor’s flag or rebranding an aid programme does not inherently improve smallholder livelihoods. Real change requires funding flexible, farmer-led initiatives tailored to local socio-ecological realities.
