stories.body:
Thatcher's Right to Buy created a generation of homeowners - did it also fuel the housing crisis?

Published 6 November 2026

Growing up in a council flat in the 1980s and 1990s, my mum would often point out homes that tenants had bought from the council. You could usually tell just from looking. A plain wooden door had been replaced with something fancier. New windows had appeared. Sometimes there was a porch or pillars outside the front door.

Those houses were bought under the Right to Buy scheme - arguably the most consequential housing policy of my lifetime. It was introduced in 1980, three years before I was born, when Margaret Thatcher's government gave council tenants in England the legal right to purchase their homes at a discounted price.

Supporters welcomed the chance for working-class families to own their own home and build wealth. Critics argue it hollowed out the country's stock of social housing and contributed to today's housing crisis.

Some of my neighbours "made a killing" from the policy, in the words of my mum. One bought an almost identical flat to ours in 1989 for £21,200, after receiving a discount of £18,800. Eight years later it sold for £54,500. Five years after that it changed hands again for £143,000. (Notably, the person who made the most money from that flat wasn't the original council tenant - it was the people who bought it afterwards.)

The writer grew up in a council flat in north London - and recently returned there, 25 years later

But Andy Burnham doesn't like the policy. The Right to Buy scheme has seen various changes since its introduction in the 1980s, and Labour has weakened it significantly since coming to power in 2024. Then, in September, the prime minister told Labour's conference: "We will reform Right to Buy. Not taking the right away from anyone in an existing home, but removing it from new homes." This would help to keep council houses in public ownership "for generations to come", Burnham told delegates.

He has previously compared trying to solve the housing crisis while continuing to sell social homes to "trying to fill a bath with the plug out".

More than 40 years after its introduction, Right to Buy remains a debate about political values as much as housing policy, balancing the home ownership ideal against the desire to preserve social housing for future generations.

A 'property-owning democracy'

Since 1980, more than two million homes have been sold through the scheme in England.

In fact, about 40% of England's council housing stock has been sold through Right to Buy. Most of those sales took place in the early years, says Prof Rebecca Tunstall, a housing academic at the University of York and London School of Economics. At the time, Labour was vehemently opposed to Thatcher's plans. Yet many of its own voters went on to benefit from them.

Labour now argues that not enough of those two million homes were replaced. Sir Keir Starmer's government restricted the scheme, including by heavily reducing the maximum discount that councils were allowed to give tenants.

And now Burnham is removing the right to buy entirely from any new-build social home. The measures are included in a bill currently making its way through Parliament. The government says that before Labour's various restrictions on the scheme, England was projected to see a net loss of 26,000 council homes over the next decade. Now there will be a net gain of 18,000 homes over the same period, it calculates.

This opens up a political divide: some opposition parties, like the Conservatives and Reform UK, say they would keep or even extend the scheme.

For those who became homeowners, Right to Buy turned a dream into reality.

Barbara Stevens, now 80, bought her two-bedroom council flat in Kentish Town, north London, through Right to Buy for around £35,000. Now mortgage-free, she estimates it could be worth between £600,000 and £700,000.

Margaret Thatcher launched Right to Buy a year after becoming prime minister, and spoke of her vision of a "property-owning democracy"

"I've always wanted to own my own property," she says.

Her friend Trevor Abrahmsohn believes her story demonstrates the success of the scheme. "If you want to condemn the poor to poverty, make them lifetime renters," he says.

Those arguments were central to Thatcher's vision of a "property-owning democracy".

Few people are more closely associated with Right to Buy than Lord Heseltine, who was the cabinet minister responsible for housing when it was introduced. When he and Thatcher launched the scheme in 1980, council tenants were offered substantial discounts to purchase their homes.

A relative of mine whose parents bought their council home in Croydon told me it was the only time "anyone would ever give you a hundred grand for free".

Even Housing Secretary Angela Rayner - part of the government that's restricting Right to Buy - bought and later sold her own council home for a profit.

In 1980, Lord Heseltine described the scheme as the biggest transfer of capital wealth from the state to ordinary people. "It certainly was," he says now, almost half a century on.

I ask him if, looking back, he would have designed the policy differently. "No," he answers.

He thinks Right to Buy gave its beneficiaries an important asset. "People who bought their own homes made a great deal of capital gain," he says.

A 'double charge' for taxpayers?

But to its detractors, Right to Buy is responsible for many of Britain's housing woes.

Prof Tunstall says the policy is partly responsible for making social housing scarcer, which meant more people competed for homes in the private rented sector, pushing up rents.

Lord Heseltine says it was originally assumed that councils would use sale proceeds to support new housing. He acknowledges that did not happen after he left government.

That failure to replace sold homes sits at the heart of the modern criticism of Right to Buy.

For Molly Harris from the New Economics Foundation, it is "private landlords [who] are the real winners".

Her think tank's research found that 41% of homes sold through Right to Buy are now privately rented out. "Homes that were built with public money, and with the aim of providing an affordable and secure path to home ownership, have since been turned into assets," Harris says.

Along with her brother (left) and other siblings, the writer says she enjoyed security in her family's rented council flat (right)

She says the shortage of social housing means more people need help with housing costs in the private rented sector, where rents are higher. So taxpayers are effectively paying twice: once to give a discount on the initial home; and then again, via housing benefit, when that home is rented out to someone who can't afford the payments. A former council home rented privately could now be valued at double, triple or quadruple what it cost when it was under local authority control.

I put that criticism to Lord Heseltine, asking him whether the scheme has failed because some ex-council homes are now effectively being rented back to the state, at higher costs.

He dismisses it as "rubbish", adding: "The scheme was wildly successful in spreading ownership across the country."

According to Harris's research, the government spent more than £58bn between 2021 and 2025 "subsidising private landlords" through the benefit system.

Newham Council says almost half of the 9,000 council homes sold under Right to Buy in Newham were later "flipped" into private rentals. The borough now has the biggest council house waiting list in the country. Last year, The Big Issue reported that Newham Council made a loss of more than £20m of taxpayers' money buying back homes it had sold just a few years earlier. The council said it was a quick way to provide new housing, and was a cheaper option than some alternatives.

And some council tenants say they are not interested in buying their homes. Ruth Crabb has lived in her flat in Havering since 1997. "I wouldn't buy my flat because I didn't want it to go out of circulation, as social housing is for those who come after me," she says. But, she adds: "I don't judge anyone who bought their property with Right to Buy."

The ownership premium

Supporters of Right to Buy also argue that you can't appreciate the true value of the scheme by looking at numbers on a spreadsheet.

The benefits of the policy extended for generations, they say, helping the children and grandchildren of those who bought homes.

Research co-authored by Matteo Sandi, an economics professor at the University of Milan, looked at children growing up in areas where Right to Buy uptake was highest. He found better educational and economic outcomes, including higher GCSE attainment, greater chances of attending university, and increased earnings in adulthood.

"What we find is that there is, in fact, a lasting benefit from growing up in an owned property," he says.

He believes it's because ownership encouraged families to invest more heavily in their homes and neighbourhoods.

One of my relatives backs this up. He tells me his parents were able to move elsewhere in the country, enjoy a better standard of living and finally afford things that had previously been out of reach. He believes Right to Buy transformed their lives.

Lord Heseltine, pictured here on a visit to Liverpool in 1981, says Right to Buy "spread ownership across the country"

But Prof Tunstall argues home ownership is not the only route to a stable family life. "The critical things for safety and for children's development and for happy families are security and affordability," she says - and children can also get that from social renting, she thinks.

Looking back, that resonates.

When I was a child and my mum rented from the council, she knew what she would be charged every month. She knew we wouldn't suddenly be forced to move. My siblings and I knew we wouldn't have to change schools. At that point, in the 1980s, one third of houses in England were council-owned. When my mum became pregnant with me, it was safe to assume that a home would soon become available - and within about a year, one did. She moved out of my nan's and into her new council flat.

The children I now meet through my work often do not have that certainty. Today, the average wait for a family-sized home in London is 27 years. Some children are moved repeatedly between hotels and hostels. Councils across England now spend £8m every day housing families in temporary accommodation.

Sandi is careful not to present his findings as an unconditional endorsement of Right to Buy.

"My take is the Right to Buy scheme was a good policy with a big limitation," he says. "More social housing should have been built."

Lots of former council estates have been partly privatised as a result of Right to Buy

But curbing Right to Buy could take a long time to bear fruit, says Prof Tunstall. Scotland abolished its Right to Buy programme in 2016 and Wales followed in 2019 - but Prof Tunstall says it "hasn't made a huge difference" yet in those nations, because the changes are too recent. (Northern Ireland continues to operate a scheme similar to Right to Buy.)

And deeper challenges will remain; Right to Buy is not the only culprit of Britain's social housing shortage, she says. Supply has also been reduced by council estate-clearance programmes, she says, which saw thousands of homes demolished from the 1990s. Like Lord Heseltine, she also blames decades of under-building: had governments continued to build at their 1980s rates, she argues, the sale of council homes might not have resulted in an overall loss of social housing.

The housing landscape has also changed dramatically since 1980. Many councils transferred responsibility over council housing to housing associations, meaning they have lost the skills and expertise to build their own stock.

More than 25 years later, I return to the street where I grew up. It looks much the same, although a few new front doors suggest more homes have been sold. My mum never took advantage of Right to Buy; she continues to rent a council flat on a small estate in south London.

I ask her if she regrets that. She says she simply wouldn't have been able to afford it.

Publicly owned rail is popular. But is it making the trains run on time? Published 13 October

I tell her that the flat she could have bought for around £20,000 would now be worth somewhere between £350,000 and £400,000.

"You're kidding?," she replies.

No-one in the 1980s could have known what would happen to house prices or the cost of living.

But whatever people think about Right to Buy, there is broad agreement on one point: the problem was not necessarily selling the homes. It was failing to replace them.

Sir Chris said it is the "legal responsibility and duty" of the executive to set a budget

Published 5 November 2026

The Northern Ireland secretary has said that it is not his "job" to set a budget and that it is the responsibility of the Northern Ireland Executive.

This comes after no resolution was reached in negotiations between executive parties and Sir Chris Bryant.

He is understood to have presented a set of conditions, including revenue raising, to be attached to any potential deal on a Stormont budget.

Sir Chris said: "They really have to take me seriously when I say there is no more money."

Seven months into this financial year the Northern Ireland Executive has still not agreed a budget.

Speaking after a series of one-to-one meetings, the First Minister Michelle O'Neill said there was still "no white smoke".

Democratic Unionist Party leader (DUP) Gavin Robinson said he felt there was a level of optimism that was "not matched by the reality inside" the room during talks.

Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant (right) greets Finance Minister John O'Dowd at Hillsborough Castle

Speaking on BBC Newsline , Sir Chris said it is the "legal responsibility and duty" of the executive to set a budget.

He described talks ending without agreement as "a bit frustrating" but added that he's still "hopeful".

He said: "I just wanted to get a move on" and added: "Whatever the total envelope is you have to live within it".

Sir Chris also said he would only set a budget for Northern Ireland if the executive parties asked him to.

"They should be able to put together their budget but they have to decide what their priorities are."

The Sinn Féin delegation was made up of Michelle O'Neill, John O'Dowd, Mary Lou McDonald and Caoimhe Archibald

After talks with the secretary of state, the first minister said that while there may be things dividing the executive, her party would persist in trying to get a budget deal done that allows public sector pay awards to be made for this year.

O'Neill also said she was getting "impatient" with the government and that she would take no lectures from it about managing finances.

Democratic Unionist Party leader Gavin Robinson said the secretary of state is "not moving"

The DUP leader said: "As it stands today, the secretary of state is not moving, the practical, honest reality of that is that without additional resource, there will not be a balanced budget".

Robinson added that "there will be no legal ability to do what it is we think the executive needs to do, and what we want it to do" without a budget.

Bryant says executive should improve 'discipline'

Stormont ministers argue the UK's devolution funding formula no longer delivers enough for them to balance their books.

The government had offered them an additional £525m this year, but they said it still left significant gaps in managing their spending pressures, particularly delivery of pay awards for public sector workers.

It is not clear what the shape of a final budget agreement could look like, with some parties insisting there is still scope to "reprofile" some of the financial package.

Bryant's conditions are believed to include the executive committing to £200m in additional revenue raising in 2027/28 and 2028/29.

He has also asked that they should improve "discipline" around promises and delivery of pay parity to public sector workers in Northern Ireland.

Health Minister Robbie Butler, UUP leader Jon Burrows and Steve Aiken spoke to the media outside Hillsborough

Ulster Unionist leader Jon Burrows said he did not want to sound "defeatist" and would continue to engage with the government.

But he said there was a real prospect that it would be resolved in time to avert the potential of strike action by health care workers waiting on pay uplifts for this year.

Speaking before talks with the secretary of state, Alliance's Agriculture Minister Andrew Muir said it is now "make your mind up time" for the executive.

"This needs to be resolved not in weeks or months, but days. We need to come to a final conclusion and give certainty to people who deserve proper pay but also in terms of investment in public services we need to get this done," he added.

Speaking on BBC NI's The View programme, Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) leader Claire Hanna said a budget is "an agreement to take responsibility and an agreement to prioritise".

Her party, which is the official opposition in the legislative assembly, is "very clear about the severe constraints," she said, but added: "the fact is by not having a budget in month eight of this financial year, everybody who's trying to operate in that budget is running at 95%".

Where are the budget negotiations at?

Talks between the government and the executive parties have been taking place for several months now , but earlier this week O'Dowd warned that a "crunch point" is approaching.

On Tuesday, the executive met again, with O'Dowd saying afterwards that he planned to present a series of options to his ministerial colleagues in the days ahead about a way forward.

He did not divulge what those may be, but the government has already said no to a request from the executive to allow a larger chunk of the money in the three-year offer to be spent this year, referred to as "front-loading".

What happens in the absence of a budget?

Without an agreed budget, departments face operating on emergency spending restricted to 95% of the prior year, with warnings that funds could run out by January.

The secretary of state has also warned that a cost-of-living £100 payment cannot be made to households in Northern Ireland until an executive budget is agreed .

That came after the government announced its first budget under Andy Burnham last week, with Northern Ireland getting an additional £270m for public services as a result, of which £131m can be used this year.

Sir Chris has said that he is exploring contingency measures to allow him to pass a budget bill at Westminster, in the event that a deal cannot be reached to do so at Stormont.

Delivering net zero also at risk, say MPs as they call for centralised policy and funding for mines and diversification

The UK is “dangerously” dependent on China for critical raw materials needed for the military, renewable energy infrastructure and AI, a parliamentary investigation has found.

MPs on the business select committee called for an urgent centralised policy and the creation of a “critical minerals finance facility” to help fund rare earth and other critical mineral mines, and deploy grants, equity and debt to accelerate a diversification programme.

“Critical minerals are the alpha of the new economy,” said the committee’s chair, Liam Byrne. “We cannot rearm Britain, build AI or deliver net zero unless we secure the minerals these technologies depend on.

“Yet 16 years after China first weaponised its chokehold over rare earths, Britain remains dangerously exposed.”

It is the second time in a week that the government’s policy on China has been criticised by Byrne’s committee.

China has a stranglehold on the world’s supply of rare earths and other critical minerals, as well as their refined byproducts that are used in everything from military jets to car-locking systems and consumer products such as fridges and washing machines.

The committee heard that “the processing stage” was where the bottlenecks were, with China dominating the refining of seven categories of minerals, including refined lithium needed for electric vehicles and rare earths used in the fuselage and wings of military aircraft to help withstand temperature extremes.

MPs were told that demand for lithium alone would increase 45-fold between 2024 and 2030, leaving the UK in a high-risk dependency relationship with China.

The demand for rare earths needed for permanent magnets used in military jets and other applications would rise 16-fold in the same period as Britain was seeking to rebuild its military capabilities.

But with China capable of suddenly turning off rare earth supplies, as it did in 2025 , a dependency on Beijing was a strategic vulnerability for the UK economy and national security, the committee found.

Separate restrictions on legacy chips after a row over a Dutch intervention in the China-owned Nexperia left the European car industry “days away” from stoppages last October.

The EU, the US and other countries faced the same risk of supplies of rare earths being cut off by China, and the committee said the UK was not putting enough effort into finding alternative supplies.

Donald Trump secured a one-year reprieve on global export restrictions on rare earths from Xi Jinping in October last year. This was extended to January 2027 after the Chinese president’s recent visit to Washington.

However, the reprieve means the UK is at the mercy of US-China relations, the report suggests.

after newsletter promotion

The most “realistic” solution was for the UK to work closely with G7 partners, the rest of Europe and Indo-Pacific countries, to “aggregate demand” and bring in new suppliers.

The committee said its investigation was frustrated by lack of transparency by the government.

“Parliament has no visibility of the capabilities the government is seeking to protect, the vulnerabilities it has identified, or the projects it is backing to reduce risk,” it said.

The committee has drawn up a 10-point plan that includes: working to identify domestic mining; refining and recycling opportunities and their costs; a strategy to encourage business to reduce procurement from China; a plan to unlock investment; and assess planning and permitting processes that may prove a barrier to mining.

As it stood, the committee said it could not be confident the government could satisfy any of its 10 tests.

“The UK requires new institutional and financial muscle,” it concluded.

A government spokesperson denied it did not have a critical minerals strategy saying it was delivering £400m “to ramp up domestic production and recycling” and forge new international partnerships. “Our strategy also sets clear goals for 2035, including meeting 10% of demand through domestic production and 20% through recycling, with no more than 60% of any critical minerals coming from any single country,” they added.

stories.title: EFF Submission to OHCHR Consultation on Child Rights and Safety in the Digital Environment
stories.summary: “ The safety of young people in the digital environment cannot be assessed without also considering the safety of young people in offline environments. For millions of young people around the world, the digital environment is their safe place, their haven from an unsafe physical environment, community, or family situation. The digital environment may be the best, perhaps only, place for them to find critical safety information and community, to explore ideas that are controversial in their families and larger physical environments, and to otherwise nourish their personal autonomy. “For these young people, regulatory efforts that limit their access to online services or to certain features they find valuable, make their lives, in total, less safe, even if there has been some marginal safety benefit to their digital environment. “The OHCHR must thus consider the whole of young persons' lives in any recommendations that come out of this process and not treat ‘safety, physical or mental health, and rights in the digital environment’ as disconnected from safety, physical or mental health, and rights elsewhere.” So begins EFF’s submission to the global Call for Inputs on Child Rights and Safety in the Digital Environment conducted by the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner on Human Rights. The OHCHR is preparing a report on the issue to be presented to the UN Human Rights Council at its 64th session in the first quarter of 2027. The Human Rights Council requested the OHCHR to solicit input from a wide range of stakeholders, including child and youth perspectives, and convene five regional consultations to assess the risks to the safety of the child in the digital environment and best practices to address these risks in different geographical areas, bearing in mind current and emerging business models. stories.title: When the Watchdogs Are Silenced: India's Crackdown on Those Documenting Online Censorship
stories.summary: On November 3, our colleagues at the Software Freedom Law Center, India (SFLC.in) received notifications from X that the Delhi Police had issued takedown requests targeting 42 URLs. Among the accounts and posts targeted were those belonging to SFLC.in , the Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF), and X account @geoblockedindia, as well as posts documenting legal notices and instances of online censorship. Takedown requests targeting SFLC.in and other digital rights groups threaten not only their work, but the public’s ability to know when and how online speech is being restricted. The requests cite grounds including hate speech, alleged defamation of the Hindu nationalist organization Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), and concerns relating to safety and security. But the context in which these requests have emerged is particularly troubling: they target organizations and individuals whose work involves documenting restrictions on online expression and making those restrictions visible to the public. In other words, the organizations being targeted are among those trying to tell the public when and how its speech is being censored. SFLC.in is one of India's most important digital rights organizations and promotes innovation and open access to knowledge by helping developers make great free and open-source software, protects privacy and civil liberties for Indians by educating and providing free legal advice, and helps policymakers make informed and just decisions about use of technology. In 2025, we recognized their work with an EFF Award for Defending Digital Freedoms. IFF (the Internet Freedom Foundation) is another of EFF's close allies in India. Like EFF, IFF combines advocacy campaigns and strategic litigation to advance digital rights. They write frequently about internet shutdowns and have filed several lawsuits contesting them. Among SFLC.in's initiatives is its Free Speech Tracker , which documents instances of online censorship, content restrictions, and account takedowns in India. In a country where government orders to restrict online content are often opaque, this work is absolutely essential. Recent legal notices object to the tracker itself, as well as the organization’s documentation of restricted content and geo-blocked material. stories.title: Reflecting on Digital Rights Wins and Losses in Sacramento
stories.summary: California’s 2026 legislative session has officially adjourned and it’s time to reflect on the wins and losses that have shaped Californians’ digital rights landscape this year. This was the second year of a two-year legislative session, which meant several bills resumed their legislative paths from 2025 . EFF monitored nearly 100 bills in the state over the two-year session. These included proposed regulations on 3D printers, access to social media platforms, police, commercial, and workplace surveillance practices, AI, and other privacy concerns. While we saw some victories, alarming developments also raised serious concerns about the future of privacy protection in the state. Celebrating Wins Use of automated decision-making and surveillance in the workplace Governor Newsom signed vital protections on the use of automated decision-making in the workplace and workplace surveillance tools, specifically No Robo Bosses ( SB 947 ) and AB 1883 . Championed by our labor partners , SB 947 limits how employers can use automated decision-making to fire or discipline workers, including provisions that ensure workers get vital information about automated decisions that affect them, and that an algorithm is not the only authority for these consequential decisions. Alongside it, AB 1883 prohibits the use of workplace surveillance to predict emotions or collect neural data. This stops employers from using potentially biased, invasive, and exploitative forms of AI surveillance at the workplace, marking an important step toward creating workplaces that respect the privacy and autonomy of workers. We look forward to continuing to ensure that technology in California’s workplaces is deployed fairly, thoughtfully, and with respect for all workers. Protecting against federal overreach EFF was also grateful to see Governor Newsom sign SB 747 , which allows damages lawsuits against federal officials who violate the U.S. Constitution . Victims of constitutional violations deserve a complete remedy and this law also helps deter constitutional violations in the first place. Gaps in current law often make it difficult to seek a damages remedy against federal officials who violate the U.S. Constitution. This bill makes it easier to bring such litigation. stories.title: Join EFF to Celebrate the Life of Aaron Swartz
stories.summary: Join us to celebrate the legacy of Aaron Swartz on Nov. 8, 2026. With the organizers of Aaron Swartz Day , we’re honoring his life with an in-person and remote hackathon. This event is supported by several organizations that carry on his work, including the Internet Archive—which is hosting the in-person event—the Freedom of the Press Foundation , Creative Commons and the Free Law Project . Aaron Swartz was a digital rights champion who believed in the need for an open internet. His life was cut short in 2013, after federal prosecutors charged him under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) for systematically downloading academic journal articles from the online database JSTOR. Facing the prospect of a long and unjust sentence, Aaron died by suicide at the age of 26. EFF was proud to call Aaron a friend and ally. We continue to stand with programmers and developers engaged in cutting-edge exploration of technology through our Coders' Rights Project . Hackathon participants can contribute code, documentation, and design to several open-source and public-interest projects. These include Secure Drop , Open Library , Quantifying the Commons , Onion Press , and our own Atlas of Surveillance . EFF Director of State Affairs Hayley Tsukayama will also join hackathon participants at the Internet Archive at 11 a.m. for an Atlas of Surveillance on-boarding session. Contributors across experience levels are welcome. The Aaron Swartz Day organizers are also open to adding new projects and workshops, so please contact them at aaronswartzday@gmail.com if you’d like to suggest a workshop or project—particularly open-source projects on Github that participants can continue to work on after the event. For more details on how to participate in-person or remotely, please visit the Aaron Swartz Day and International Hackathon page at www.aaronswartzday.org .
